title: Beside the weeping
hook: sit with a grieving friend and sigh with them, but don't groan inside; some readers find this cool, others wise (Enchiridion 16)

segments.voice: Yesterday: symposion, life as a banquet. Your line was when the dish comes. Did you take a modest share of something and pass the rest along? Day three hundred forty-eight.

Lifeguards learn a hard rule early. When someone is drowning, you don't just leap in and grab them. A panicking swimmer can pull the rescuer under, and then there are two people in trouble instead of one. You go in with a float, you stay on top of the water, and from there you can actually help. Grief can work like deep water. A friend calls, sobbing, and it's easy to dive straight in, until we're crying too hard to hear what they need. Section sixteen of the handbook is about exactly this moment. Today: beside the weeping.
screen: `THE LIFEGUARD'S RULE.` → `TWO IN THE WATER.` → `BESIDE THE WEEPING.`

segments.voice: First, the scene. When you see someone weeping in grief, Epictetus says, because a child has gone far away, or because they've lost their property, don't let the impression carry you off, as if they were truly in the grip of an outside evil. Second, the inner sentence. Have ready, he says, the thought: it isn't the event itself that crushes this person, since someone else meets the same event and isn't crushed. It's their judgment about it. That's day three hundred thirty-seven, dogma, turned toward someone else. Third, the outward part. And yet, he says, don't hesitate to sympathize with them in words, and even, if the moment calls for it, to sigh and groan along with them. Only take care not to groan inwardly as well. Sit with them. Speak gently. Just don't drown. Fourth, the two readings. Some people find this passage cool, even a little false: comforting someone while privately thinking their grief is a mistake. Others find it wise and practical, the lifeguard's float: you stay steady enough to stay present, to bring soup on day fifteen, to call again in a month. Epictetus himself doesn't tell you to say the inner sentence out loud. That would be cruel, and nothing in the text suggests it. Neighbors have their own words for the outward part. Paul's letter to the Romans, in the King James words: "weep with them that weep." Epictetus pairs that outward part with a steady one inside.
screen: `SOMEONE WEEPING IN GRIEF.` · `INSIDE: NOT THE EVENT, THE JUDGMENT.` · `OUTSIDE: SIGH WITH THEM.` · `COOL, OR WISE?` · then, large: `WITH THEM, STEADY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you know who is hurting right now. Picture sitting beside them. Let your face soften. Let real sympathy come, the kind you'd show. Then, underneath, find your own feet. Feel the floor, feel your breath going in and out, steady. Two things at once: warmth on the outside, ground on the inside. If you like, decide one small thing you could do for them this week. The bell holds the time.
Paul, who wrote weep with them that weep: sigh with a grieving friend, sympathize in words, but keep steady inside, so you can stay. Today's word.
Your line: with them, steady. When someone brings you their trouble today, give them your warmth and keep your feet on the floor. Day three hundred forty-eight.

screen: `DAY 348 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: AN ACTOR IN A PLAY.`

howItsDone: Some people who practice Stoicism comfort the grieving with real warmth in word and gesture while trying to stay inwardly steady, so they can keep showing up.

fork.setup: your friend is weeping because their child has moved far away. what does section sixteen suggest?
options: tell them it's only their opinion.
sympathize aloud, and stay steady inside.
fork.reveal: don't hesitate to sympathize, even to sigh with them, Epictetus says; just don't groan inwardly too.

trapdoor: what you thought: don't get emotional.
what it means: sympathize openly with someone grieving, while keeping steady inside so you can stay with them.
what a scholar hears: the inner thought applies Enchiridion 5 to someone else; the same verb, to groan (stenazein), names the outward groan he allows and the inward one he warns against.

notes: Review (2026-10-01): 'the steady part is what Epictetus adds' read as a comparison against Romans 12:15, now neutral; trapdoor's unverified claim about Simplicius replaced with a detail from the text; softened 'part of us dives straight in'.

The text names a child gone abroad and lost property; the script keeps to those two.
